blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ACE-inhibitor/ARB adverse-effect teaching
stem: A client stopped lisinopril because of a persistent ACE-inhibitor cough and is starting losartan. Which teaching about cough is most accurate?

options.A: A previous ACE-inhibitor cough makes losartan contraindicated even without angioedema or hypersensitivity because the cough predicts a similar ARB class reaction.
options.B: Losartan can also cause cough, and in patients with previous ACE-inhibitor cough its frequency is expected to remain close to lisinopril, so the switch offers little cough-related benefit.
options.C: If cough develops after the switch, it should generally be considered unrelated to losartan because ARB therapy has not been linked to recurrent medication-associated cough in this setting.
options.D: Cough can still occur with losartan, but in controlled trials of patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough it was substantially less frequent with losartan than with lisinopril.

rationale: Current losartan labeling describes two randomized controlled trials in hypertensive patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough. Cough occurred in 17% of losartan-treated clients versus 69% with lisinopril in one trial and 29% versus 62% in the other; the label also reports postmarketing cough cases, including positive rechallenges. Therefore D is the best answer: cough can still occur with losartan, but it was substantially less frequent than with lisinopril in these trials. A is incorrect because prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a listed losartan contraindication. B contradicts the controlled-trial findings. C incorrectly dismisses losartan as a possible contributor to cough despite trial cough events and postmarketing positive rechallenges.
educational_objective: Teach clients switched from an ACE inhibitor to losartan that cough is substantially less frequent with losartan than with lisinopril in trials of patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough, but cough can still occur and should not automatically be dismissed.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine); packager: Lupin Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
source_document_title: Losartan Potassium Tablets, for oral use — Prescribing Information
source_locator: Full Prescribing Information §6.1 Clinical Trials Experience > Cough: two controlled trials in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough; Study 1 cough 17% losartan vs 69% lisinopril, Study 2 29% vs 62%; cases of cough including positive rechallenges reported postmarketing. §4 Contraindications: hypersensitivity to any component and coadministration with aliskiren in patients with diabetes; prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not listed.
source_claim_supported: In patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough, controlled trials showed substantially less cough with losartan than with lisinopril; cough can still occur with losartan, and prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a listed contraindication.
blueprint_locator: Printed p. 38, Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: review pertinent data prior to medication administration; educate client about medications; evaluate client response to medication; assess and teach about medication side/adverse effects.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Removed the isolated absolute-word distractor pattern and rewrote all four choices as clinically plausible teaching statements.
Balanced option lengths so the correct answer is no longer uniquely longest while preserving one source-supported best answer.
audit_note: Clinical content was re-audited from zero after revision. D matches the current controlled-trial and postmarketing labeling. A invents a contraindication from prior ACE-inhibitor cough, B contradicts the comparative trial rates, and C incorrectly excludes losartan as a possible cough contributor. No second defensible answer or material cueing remains.
